entry.title: Clifton Bricks Pty Limited v Gerlach [2003] NSWCA 257
entry.content:

entry.title: HYDE -v- SOUTH METROPOLITAN HEALTH SERVICE [2026] WADC 102
entry.content:
Sarah Hyde applied under s 39 of the Limitation Act 2005 (WA) to extend time to bring a medical negligence claim against South Metropolitan Health Service over alleged over-tightening of a CAM boot in 2019 causing nerve injury. The District Court granted the extension, finding she became aware of the physical cause of her injury only on receipt of Dr Sekel’s expert report dated 19 December 2023, not from earlier hospital records or a lay JobSeeker comment.

Key holding: Under s 39 of the Limitation Act 2005 (WA), awareness of a physical cause and attribution requiring expert medical knowledge ordinarily arises from an expert opinion reasonably capable of acceptance, not mere suspicion or lay opinion.

As McLure P said in AME, awareness of the matters in s 39(4)(a) and s 39(4)(b) of the Act depends on inferences from the primary facts drawn by a medical expert.

entry.title: Brighton Ceiling Pty Ltd v Pocrnja & Ors [2005] NSWCA 175
entry.content:
The NSW Court of Appeal considered whether a workers compensation indemnity claimant could include non-economic loss in notional motor accident damages under s 151Z of the Workers Compensation Act ([2005] NSWCA 175). Because excluding that component would not change the claimant’s recovery, the Court treated the issue as hypothetical and reinstated the arbitrator’s award unchanged. No exact damages amount is stated.

Key holding: A court need not determine whether non-economic loss may be included in notional motor accident damages under s 151Z where excluding that component would not affect the claimant’s recovery.

The Court held the question was hypothetical because even excluding the non-economic loss component would not affect the claimant's recovery, and reinstated the arbitrator's award without modification.

entry.title: GUPTA v ROBERTSON [2026] SADC 130
entry.content:
The applicant claimed damages for a right-knee injury or aggravation allegedly caused by a low-speed rear-end collision, with negligence admitted. The Court found the collision caused only a minor, temporary exacerbation of a pre-existing 2015 motorcycle injury and dismissed the claim, with the s 124AC set-off reducing compensable loss to nil.

Key holding: Where a plaintiff alleges that a collision aggravated or exacerbated a pre-existing condition, factual causation under s 34(1)(a) requires proof on the balance of probabilities that that particular aggravation or exacerbation would not have occurred but for the defendant’s negligence.

Where the harm alleged is an aggravation or exacerbation of a pre-existing condition, the relevant inquiry under section 34(1)(a) is whether Mr Gupta has proved, on the balance of probabilities, that the particular aggravation or exacerbation would not have occurred but for Ms Robertson's negligence.

entry.title: Hovius v Speno Rail Maintenance Australia Pty Ltd [2026] NSWSC 1152
entry.content:
Mr Hovius sought judicial review of a Personal Injury Commission Medical Appeal Panel decision assessing his permanent impairment at 18% after workplace knee/hip injuries and scarring. The Supreme Court found the Appeal Panel failed to assess impairment in accordance with the workers compensation guidelines, failed to address all appeal grounds including pain and hip, and failed to give adequate reasons. The Court held he was entitled to the relief sought, including an extension of time.

Key holding: The workers compensation guidelines have delegated legislative force, and an Appeal Panel’s failure to assess permanent impairment in accordance with them can amount to a constructive failure to exercise jurisdiction.

Those guidelines have the force or effect of delegated legislation and failure to carry out an assessment in accordance with them may constitute a constructive failure to exercise jurisdiction.

entry.title: Frazer v State of Queensland [2026] QSC 82 (22 April 2026)
entry.content:
Ms Frazer, an experienced teacher, sued the State of Queensland after suffering PTSD following an incident where an aggrieved parent attended the school looking to confront her. The State admitted it owed a non-delegable duty of care to Ms Frazer, but disputed breach. The court found no breach and entered judgment for the defendant.

Key holding: A policy authorising physical force to remove an abusive or threatening person does not require force in every circumstance; reasonableness depends on the unfolding situation.

It seems to me that the authorisation in Chief Executive Guideline No 1 of 2012 to take all reasonable steps including physical force to eject an abusive, threatening or disorderly person does not, could not and should not demand in all circumstances that physical force be used to eject an abusive, threatening or disorderly person.

entry.title: Gong v AWI Steel Pty Limited [2026] NSWSC 331 (9 April 2026)
entry.content:
Mr Gong, a boilermaker/welder supplied to AWI Steel’s factory via labour-hire arrangements, was injured when a heavy steel plate slipped and fell on his foot. He sued AWI in negligence; AWI denied duty/breach and alleged contributory negligence. The Supreme Court found AWI liable but reduced damages for Mr Gong’s contributory negligence, with AWI bearing the greater responsibility.

Key holding: A principal or occupier that organises, controls and supervises work at its premises owes a duty of reasonable care to independent contractor workers to avoid unnecessary risk of injury.

AWI's duty being to use reasonable care to avoid unnecessary risk of injury to all those who worked together at its factory, including the Ebenezer workers, given the risk of harm to which they were exposed, given the work AWI' had them perform there.

entry.title: Kwiatkowski v Plum Pictures Limited (No 3) [2026] NSWSC 288 (31 March 2026)
entry.content:
This procedural ruling concerns a personal injury claim stayed because the plaintiff seeks to advance an alternative work injury damages claim without complying with Chapter 7 of the Workplace Injury Management and Workers Compensation Act 1998 (NSW). The first defendant sought dismissal or strike-out, but the Court refused immediate dismissal and instead stayed the proceedings to allow compliance. The decision turned on the discretionary consequences of non-compliance.

Key holding: Non-compliance with Chapter 7 of the WIM Act does not automatically require dismissal; the court retains a discretion whether to dismiss, taking into account factors including the defendant’s conduct, prejudice, delay and the overriding purpose.

The effect of the authorities adverted to above is to preserve the discretion of the Court as to whether a proceeding should be dismissed for lack of compliance. Non-compliance may erect a procedural barrier to final relief, but not necessarily so, as the result in Berowra Holdings demonstrates.

entry.title: Bath v Allianz Australia Insurance Limited [2026] NSWSC 165 (9 March 2026)
entry.content:
Mr Bath sought judicial review of a Personal Injury Commission review panel decision that assessed his whole person impairment at 5%, below the >10% threshold for non-economic loss damages under s 4.11 of the Motor Accident Injuries Act 2017 (NSW). The panel found his left shoulder injury was not caused by a 2019 Sydney Light Rail accident. The Supreme Court set aside the decision for jurisdictional error because the panel treated the absence of contemporaneous shoulder complaints as decisive on causation.

Key holding: A review panel commits jurisdictional error if it treats the absence of documented contemporaneous complaints as decisive or determinative of causation, rather than determining contribution on the whole evidence.

By treating the absence of documented contemporaneous complaints as decisive, the Panel failed properly to exercise its jurisdiction.

entry.title: Anderson v Claytons Towing Service Pty Ltd & Ors [2026] QSC 26 (5 March 2026)
entry.content:
This Supreme Court of Queensland decision concerns a tow truck driver injured when a bus he was preparing to tow rolled off wooden blocks onto him. The court found the bus owner released the handbrake despite instructions, making him negligent, and that the injury fell within Queensland’s motor accident insurance scheme. The third party notice was dismissed.

Key holding: Under s 5(1)(a)(iii) of the Motor Accident Insurance Act 1994 (Qld), a vehicle is running out of control when it moves while no person is in a position to steer it or apply the brakes, even if it is not being driven.

However, in my view, a vehicle is running out of control if it is moves when there is no one in a position either to steer the movement or inhibit the movement by applying the brakes. That was the position when this bus moved off the wooden blocks.

entry.title: Ypermachou v PMK Pty Ltd [2026] NSWSC 149 (4 March 2026)
entry.content:
Mr Ypermachou sought judicial review of a Personal Injury Commission Appeal Panel decision confirming medical assessment certificates for permanent impairment under the Table of Disabilities and whole person impairment. He alleged the Appeal Panel failed to address a clearly articulated submission about right-ankle/gait evidence and gave inadequate reasons, particularly regarding sleep apnoea. entry.title: Ardis-Phasey v Neal & Anor [2026] QDC 25 (27 February 2026)
entry.content:
The plaintiff was injured in a motor vehicle accident at age 14 and later sued for damages; liability was admitted, leaving quantum in issue. The District Court accepted his evidence of chronic lower back pain and assessed damages under the Civil Liability Act 2003 (Qld) and the Civil Liability Regulation 2003 (Qld). The court awarded $182,800, including general damages, future economic loss, future treatment and out-of-pocket expenses.

Key holding: In assessing future economic loss, the court compensates loss of earning capacity, and a comparison of actual and hypothetical wages is only one available method; a global assessment may be used.

The rate of wage likely to be earned as compared to the wage which could have been earned without the injury in some current job is a way of calculating damages flowing from that loss, but the actual versus hypothetical wages calculation is not the only way to measure the loss. A matter of principle, I am identifying loss of capacity and the economic consequences of that loss of capacity for this particular young man with this injury.

entry.title: Tazleem v Certain Underwriters at Lloyds Listed in Annexure �eoeA�e� [2026] NSWSC 124 (26 February 2026)
entry.content:
The plaintiff was injured at Better Truck Repairs Pty Ltd’s premises when an excavator bucket detached from forklift tines. He sued BTR’s public liability insurer and the Workers Compensation Nominal Insurer standing in for deregistered labour hire company JPBC. The central fight was whether the plaintiff was BTR’s employee (excluded by the policy) or JPBC’s employee (policy responded), with contributory negligence and damages also in issue.

Key holding: In a labour hire arrangement, the true employer for insurance purposes may be the labour hire company where the commercial and contractual framework provides that workers placed with the host become its employees, notwithstanding the host’s recruitment and setting of work conditions.

In conclusion, I am satisfied that the commercial scenario in which BTR and JPBC operated meant that upon the plaintiff being accepted as suitable for the position at BTR, that the plaintiff then became an employee of JPBC.
